argument: The episode is a practical field guide to the small set of logical fallacies that recur across almost every everyday disagreement, regardless of topic. The point is not just to feel that an argument is wrong but to be able to name the specific flawed move being made, since most disagreements recycle the same 10-15 fallacious patterns.
keyIdeas: Appeal to consequences becomes fallacious specifically when it's used to argue for the factual truth of a claim, not when used to argue for the practical value of adopting a policy or action.
Affirming the consequent mistakes 'if P then Q, and Q is true' for proof that P is true, ignoring that Q could have many other possible causes besides P.
Appeal to ignorance treats absence of disproof as evidence of truth; its personal incredulity variant substitutes 'I can't imagine how this could be true' for actual evidence.

A slippery-slope fallacy asserts a chain of increasingly extreme consequences without establishing that each link is actually likely, unlike a legitimate causal-chain argument that justifies every step.
Strawman, ad hominem, false equivalence, and bandwagon fallacies each substitute a distorted, personal, superficial, or headcount-based move for actually engaging with the substance of an argument.

terms.def: Arguing that a claim is true (or false) because believing it produces a desirable (or undesirable) outcome, rather than because of evidence for its truth.
Invalidly concluding that the antecedent of a true conditional must be true just because its consequent is observed to be true.
Treating the absence of disproof as evidence that a claim is true; its personal incredulity variant treats one's own inability to imagine something as disproof.
Arguing a position is bad because it will set off a chain of increasingly extreme consequences, without justifying that each link in the chain is actually likely.
Misrepresenting an opponent's position as weaker or more extreme than it actually is, then refuting that weaker version instead.
Treating two things as comparably valid based on one superficial similarity while ignoring real differences in the evidence behind each.
